house.redistricting_notes: Mid-decade redraws reshaped ~8 states. Texas: legislature drew 5 new R-leaning seats (incl. new TX-9, TX-32, TX-35); a federal panel enjoined the map Nov 18, 2025 but SCOTUS stayed and then allowed it 6-3 on Dec 4, 2025. California: Prop 50 passed with ~64% (Nov 2025), redrawing to target 5 GOP seats (CA-1, CA-3, CA-22, CA-41/CA-48 area, CA-6 now D+5; new CA-38). Florida: special session map signed May 4, 2026 targeting 3-5 R gains (new FL-22; FL-9 Soto and FL-14 Castor now in R-leaning seats). North Carolina: Oct 2025 redraw made NC-1 (Don Davis) R+5. Ohio: unanimous compromise map (Oct 2025) made OH-1 more competitive, OH-9 more R, OH-13 more D. Louisiana: after Louisiana v. Callais (Apr 2026) a map signed May 29 eliminated one of two Black-plurality D seats (LA-6). Alabama: new map removes AL-2's D lean (now R+7); state court block stayed by SCOTUS Jun 2, 2026. Tennessee: TN-9 (Memphis) split, now Safe R. Utah: court-ordered map creates a safe-D Salt Lake seat (UT-1). Virginia: Democrats' redistricting amendment invalidated May 8, 2026 (old lines). Missouri: 2025 map targeting MO-5 blocked by referendum; 2022 map in place. Maryland, Indiana, Kansas efforts failed; Wisconsin challenge dismissed Mar 31, 2026; SCOTUS blocked an NY-11 redraw. Net on-paper effect: roughly R +6 to +9 (TX, FL, NC, OH, AL, LA, TN) offset by D +5 to +6 (CA, UT), i.e. about R +1 to +4 net, but forecasters (DDHQ, Silver) conclude Republicans gain little or nothing net because the strong D environment flips several of the new marginal R seats; the main effect is fewer true swing seats (Silver: D gain ~22 seats on average despite a ~D+9 environment).

method.note: Prior per race = weighted blend of our polling average, published model probabilities, race ratings, prediction markets and fundamentals (2024 presidential margin plus the national shift implied by the generic ballot, with an incumbency bonus). On election night the prior is blended with the live count, weighted by the share of expected vote in, and shifted by the median gap between results and expectations in races that are mostly counted. Chamber odds come from 20,000 simulations with a shared national error term. Indicative only.
